structured_output.differences: The author's c1–c4 match my step-1 reading closely. My reading separated out an implicit \"is a folder\" condition and an implicit uniqueness expectation (\"the folder\" implies exactly one match), neither of which the author lists explicitly — but both are naturally folded into c1's phrasing and the definite article, not separate testable conditions. No substantive gap exists between the author's conditions and a careful reading of the request.

ambiguity_effects.phrase: under Client Deliverables (direct child vs. any nested descendant)
ambiguity_effects.explain: In general usage this phrase could plausibly include deeply nested folders, not just direct children. In this dataset, however, every folder inside Client Deliverables is a direct child (no further nesting exists), so the two readings pick out the same set of candidates.
All modified_at values in the dataset fall in 2026, so context resolves this without real ambiguity — there's no other plausible year to consider.

ambiguity_effects.phrase: hasn't been modified since May 1 (inclusive vs. exclusive of May 1 itself)
ambiguity_effects.explain: Whether a modification exactly on May 1 would count as passing or failing is genuinely unclear in isolation, but no record in the data has modified_at falling exactly on May 1, so this boundary question never actually arises here.

ambiguity_effects.phrase: modified (folder's own metadata vs. changes to its contents)
ambiguity_effects.explain: A careful reader could wonder whether adding/editing files inside a folder should count as "modifying" it. The dataset only exposes a single modified_at field per folder with no separate content-change signal, so this distinction can't be tested and doesn't affect which folder matches.

ambiguity_effects.phrase: larger than 2 GB (decimal GB vs. binary GiB)
ambiguity_effects.explain: 2GB as 2,000,000,000 bytes vs. 2,147,483,648 bytes (2^31) would matter near the boundary, but every candidate is comfortably on one side or the other (1.9GB/50MB/80MB clearly fail, 2.2GB+ clearly pass under both readings), so the ambiguity doesn't change the outcome.

ambiguity_effects.phrase: has a shared link on it (currently active vs. any historical link)
ambiguity_effects.explain: A careful reader might wonder if a since-disabled shared link would still count. The dataset only encodes presence or absence of a shared_link object with no "disabled but once existed" state, so this distinction isn't exercised by the data.
